clinicalPearls: Reticulate red-brown pigmentation with telangiectasia and fine atrophy over the sides of the neck, the cheeks and the upper chest
Characteristically spares the shaded skin under the chin (the submental shadow), underlining its photo-aggravated nature
Chronic cumulative sun exposure is the principal driver, with photosensitising fragrances and cosmetics thought to contribute
More common in fair-skinned, middle-aged to elderly individuals, particularly women
It combines a vascular (telangiectatic erythema) and a pigmentary component, so treatment often needs both vascular and pigment-directed laser or intense pulsed light
Photoprotection and avoiding perfumed products on the area help limit progression
The term poikiloderma denotes the triad of atrophy, telangiectasia and mottled pigmentation
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic ultraviolet exposure of the lateral neck and upper chest produces dermal elastosis, dilatation of superficial blood vessels (telangiectasia) and irregular melanin distribution together with epidermal atrophy, giving the poikilodermatous appearance. Photosensitising ingredients in fragrances and cosmetics are believed to augment the ultraviolet damage. The area beneath the chin is shielded from direct sunlight and is therefore characteristically spared.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination noting sparing of the submental shadow
Dermoscopy to assess the vascular and pigmentary components
Patch or photopatch testing where a photoallergy is suspected
Skin biopsy if a connective tissue disease such as dermatomyositis is being considered
redFlags: Poikiloderma accompanied by muscle weakness or other features suggesting dermatomyositis
An atypical distribution not corresponding to sun-exposed sites
Rapidly evolving changes prompting exclusion of a systemic disorder
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign, chronic and mainly of cosmetic importance; laser or intense pulsed light can markedly improve appearance, but it tends to progress without diligent photoprotection.
pitfalls: Overlooking poikiloderma associated with dermatomyositis or another connective tissue disease
Treating only the pigment and ignoring the vascular telangiectatic component
Failing to address ongoing sun exposure and fragrance contact
Confusing it with melasma or rosacea
management: Rigorous daily broad-spectrum photoprotection and sun avoidance to limit progression, the cornerstone of management
Avoid perfumed and photosensitising cosmetics applied to the neck and chest
Vascular-selective laser or intense pulsed light to target the telangiectatic erythema component
Pigment-directed laser or intense pulsed light to address the dyspigmentation
Realistic counselling that the condition is benign and largely cosmetic, with recurrence likely without sustained photoprotection
Dermatology referral for device-based treatment and to exclude a connective tissue disease mimic such as dermatomyositis where features are atypical
